title: Constant-factor edit-distance approximation in \(O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
formal: Do absolute constants \(C\ge 1, K>0\) and \(d\ge 0\) and a uniform randomized classical algorithm exist that, for every two length-n strings x,y, output an integer D satisfying \(ED(x,y)\le D\le C\cdot ED(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) in at most \(Kn(\log _{2}(n+2))^{d}\) time?
definitions: Use the unit-cost Levenshtein distance: ED is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming x into y; matching equal symbols costs zero. The input consists of \(n\ge 1\) and two explicitly stored arrays \(x,y\in \{0,\ldots ,n^{2}+1\}^{n}\). This fixes an integer alphabet whose symbols fit in \(O(\log  n)\) bits and includes binary and fixed finite alphabets. Computation is on a word RAM with word length \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) for an absolute constant B, using random access, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic at unit cost. The algorithm may draw independent random bits, but has no input-dependent advice, preprocessed database or oracle. All preprocessing counts toward the bound, which must hold on every execution. Success is required separately for every input pair. Output only the distance estimate; an edit script is not required. The constants C,K,d,B are fixed independently of n and the strings. There is no promise about the distance, repetitions or input distribution, and no additive error is allowed. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: Determines whether a universal constant loss in accuracy makes the basic string-alignment metric computable with only polylogarithmic overhead beyond input reading.

importance.reason: A central remaining precision–runtime boundary for edit distance, distinct from the established n^{1+ε} constant-factor algorithms and from exact-computation hardness.

progress.text: Andoni–Onak give subpolynomial distortion in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time.
Backurs–Indyk establish SETH-based hardness for strongly subquadratic exact edit distance; this does not rule out constant approximation.
Koucký–Saks prove a constant-factor guarantee on sufficiently distant pairs, with an additive term on general inputs.
Andoni–Nosatzki obtain constant approximation for arbitrary pairs in \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) time for each fixed \(\varepsilon\); July 2022 revision states the parameter dependence.
Mao–Rubinstein post their STOC 2026 approximation schemes, with near-exact accuracy and a quasipolynomial speedup over quadratic time.
The Andoni–Nosatzki journal article is published online; its runtime remains \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\), rather than n polylog n.

status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No \(O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\)-time, fixed-constant approximation for all input pairs was found in the checked primary sources. The August 2026 journal publication gives \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) time, and the STOC 2026 approximation scheme targets a different runtime–accuracy regime.

context_blocks.text: Insertions and deletions make alignment the central difficulty. If a symbol is inserted near the start of a string, many later positions shift, even when almost all symbols are unchanged. Comparing corresponding positions can therefore report many mismatches while a short edit sequence exists. The task is to estimate the best alignment cost without inspecting the full quadratic dynamic-programming table.

For example, deleting the first symbol of an alternating binary string and reinserting it at the end produces an equal-length string with almost every position changed, but edit distance at most two. A Hamming-distance estimate can be linear in the length on this pair. This illustrates why a simple positional comparison cannot provide a universal constant-factor approximation.

The multiplicative guarantee is deliberately strict at small distances. When \(x=y\), success requires \(D=0\). When the true distance is one, the returned value must remain bounded by the same universal C used on arbitrarily long strings. An additive error such as \(n^{0.9}\) can be acceptable for very distant strings while being arbitrarily poor on these nearby pairs. Reading both complete strings is allowed; this is not a sublinear-query problem.

Early algorithms already showed that one could gain substantial speed by allowing larger distortion. Andoni–Onak obtain a subpolynomial approximation factor \(2^{\widetilde{O} (\sqrt{\log  n})}\) in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time, with a STOC 2009 precursor and a later journal version. Both quantities improve substantially on older polynomial approximations, but the factor still grows with input length.

Koucký–Saks obtain a constant-factor result for sufficiently distant pairs, with an additive \(n^{1- \zeta}\) term in the general guarantee. The exponent \(\zeta\) and the multiplicative constant depend on the fixed runtime parameter. Their theorem makes the missing regime explicit: the additive term cannot be absorbed into a constant times the true distance on every pair.

Andoni–Nosatzki remove that distance promise. Their Theorem 1.1 gives, for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\), an \(O(n^{1+\varepsilon})\)-time randomized algorithm with approximation \(f(1/\varepsilon )\). The manuscript notes doubly exponential dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\). Its FOCS 2020 result was revised on arXiv in July 2022 and published in SIAM Journal on Computing in August 2026. The recent publication date does not change the quantified \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) guarantee into n times a polylogarithm.

The order of these choices is decisive. A fixed \(\varepsilon =0.01\) gives a fixed approximation factor, but \(n^{0.01}\) eventually exceeds every fixed power of log n. Choosing \(\varepsilon\) as a function of n to force the desired runtime also changes the approximation factor and the hidden constants. The theorem does not provide the single constant C required here. This is a quantitative gap within already very fast approximation algorithms, rather than a question about whether any strongly subquadratic constant approximation exists.

Mao–Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 work improves a different part of the tradeoff. For every fixed accuracy parameter \(\eta >0\), it gives a randomized \((1+\eta )\)-approximation in \(n^{2}/2^{\log ^{\Omega (1)}n}\) time. The approximation can be arbitrarily close to exact, but the displayed speedup is over the quadratic scale, not down to n polylog n. It does not resolve this card’s constant-factor, much-faster-runtime target.

Backurs–Indyk’s SETH-based barrier concerns exact computation in strongly subquadratic time. It should not be applied indiscriminately to approximation: the known constant-factor algorithms already run in that regime. An impossibility result for the present question would need to preserve a multiplicative gap of the appropriate size while respecting the randomized model and the very small runtime overhead.

The card concerns ordinary strings and numerical estimation. Tree edit distance, distances between languages, weighted edit operations and quantum algorithms each change the problem. Likewise, an efficient nearest-neighbour data structure with substantial preprocessing does not immediately yield the stated two-string algorithm. These distinctions keep the target useful as a precise benchmark for the algorithmic complexity of a basic sequence metric.

A positive resolution would show that constant distortion suffices to reduce this alignment problem to essentially the cost of reading its input, up to logarithmic factors. Even a large universal approximation constant would settle that structural issue. Reducing the constant, producing an alignment, and obtaining practical implementations would remain meaningful subsequent goals.

The separate card TCS-7220 asks whether every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) permits a \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation in \(O(n^{2- \delta _{\varepsilon}})\) time for some fixed \(\delta _{\varepsilon}>0\). Its near-exact guarantee does not by itself provide this card’\(s O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) runtime, while this card’s unspecified constant factor does not supply arbitrary \(1+\varepsilon\) accuracy. The user explicitly approved retaining both targets on 11 September 2026.

sentences: Edit distance counts the cheapest sequence of insertions, deletions, and substitutions transforming one string into another.
The reviewed question asks for a randomized universal constant-factor approximation in near-linear time.
Insertions can shift many positions, making direct coordinate comparisons misleading even when edit distance is tiny.
The target would estimate global alignment cost without constructing the full quadratic dynamic-programming table.
The guarantee is purely multiplicative, so identical strings must yield zero and nearby strings cannot be hidden behind a large additive error.
